title: The Story So Far
blurb: Reflect on life events and choices

steps.html:
Four people describe a decision that turned out well, and none of them says it was planned. Then a family that produced a Duke, a Chancellor and a Prime Minister — and a film that keeps asking what would have happened if one of them had chosen differently.

  • Follow four people reflecting on a decision
  • Use the language of looking back
  • Watch a documentary about a family across three centuries
  • Write a short biography

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: 'In retrospect, losing my job was a blessing in disguise.'
steps.prompt: What is the phrase in retrospect doing?
options: Saying that the speaker knew at the time.
Marking the judgement as one made afterwards, not at the time.
Softening a criticism of the employer.
steps.answer: Marking the judgement as one made afterwards, not at the time.
steps.why: In retrospect and with hindsight both do this, and both are essential to writing about a life.

steps.title: Writing about a life that could have gone otherwise
steps.html:
Recycled from Lessons 45 and 46, put to work in a biography — the last grammar screen of the level.

Any account of a life turns on decisions, and English marks those with the forms you have just learned. A biography without conditionals reads as a list of dates.

Third conditional for the turning point: If he hadn't died in 1883, many thought he could have become Prime Minister. Note could have rather than would have — the writer is not claiming certainty.

Mixed conditional for a past cause still visible now: If he hadn't won that battle, the area could look quite different today.

If it weren't for / if it hadn't been for + noun, for a single decisive factor: He would probably never have become Prime Minister if it weren't for the outbreak of war.

Wish and if only for the subject's own view, when you have it: She wishes she had applied again. Do not put a wish into somebody's head that they never expressed.

And the register markers: in retrospect, with hindsight, at the time, as it turned out, who knows. These separate what was known then from what is known now, which is the whole difficulty of writing about a life.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences, most of them from the film you are about to watch.

If he hadn't, the area could have looked quite different today.
Third conditional, softened with could.

Many thought he could even have become Prime Minister if he hadn't died in 1883.
Result first, condition second — no comma.

He would probably have never become Prime Minister if it weren't for the outbreak of war.
A single decisive factor.

If he hadn't been born into such a powerful family, who knows?
The condition stated, the result refused.

History could have been very different.
A third conditional result with no if clause.

In retrospect, losing my job was a blessing in disguise.
A judgement made afterwards.

With hindsight I should never have started.
Should have for a past mistake.

I couldn't have wished for a better course.
A fixed phrase, and a third conditional in form.

Thank goodness I didn't listen to my parents.
Relief at a course not taken.

What's done is done.
Refusing the counterfactual altogether.

steps.title: Writing one life event three ways
steps.html:
1. The fact: she was made redundant from an advertising job, and she now works freelance and is happier.
  2. Neutral: She was made redundant in 2019 and has worked freelance since. Accurate, and it says nothing.
  3. With the judgement marked: In retrospect, being made redundant was a blessing in disguise. The reader now knows this is hindsight.
  4. With the counterfactual: If she hadn't been made redundant, she would probably still be in the same office. Mixed conditional — past cause, present result.
  5. And softened, if you are not sure: If she hadn't been made redundant, who knows? The film uses exactly this move about Winston Churchill.

steps.title: Dynasty – The Churchills
steps.sub: Dynasty – The Churchills. About seven minutes.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.sub: Four items.
steps.prompt: Why was Blenheim Palace built?
options: As a reward from Queen Anne to John Churchill for his military victories.
As a monument to Winston Churchill.
steps.answer: As a reward from Queen Anne to John Churchill for his military victories.
steps.why: He became the first Duke of Marlborough in 1702 and won the Battle of Blenheim in 1704.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.sub: Four items.
steps.prompt: Why did Winston's father Randolph go into politics?
options: He inherited the title and the duties that went with it.
His elder brother became the eighth Duke, so he had to pursue a different career path.
He was asked to stand by the family's political patrons.
steps.answer: His elder brother became the eighth Duke, so he had to pursue a different career path.
steps.why: He became Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.sub: Four items.
steps.prompt: What does the film say about Winston becoming Prime Minister?
options: It was inevitable from birth, given the family he was born into.
He would probably never have become Prime Minister if it weren't for the outbreak of the Second World War.
He was elected to the office on his first attempt at it.
steps.answer: He would probably never have become Prime Minister if it weren't for the outbreak of the Second World War.
steps.why: 'Suddenly, the country needed somebody who could stand up to the enemy.'

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.sub: Four items.
steps.prompt: How does the film end?
options: With a list of his achievements and nothing else at all.
With a conditional: if he hadn't been born into such a family, history could have been very different.
With his funeral, and the crowds that turned out for it.
steps.answer: With a conditional: if he hadn't been born into such a family, history could have been very different.
steps.why: 'Who knows?' — the film declines to answer its own question.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.prompt: The film says Churchill was voted the Greatest Briton of All Time, and then immediately says his success 'didn't come from nowhere'. Why?
options: To argue that the poll was wrong and the result undeserved.
To set up the whole film: the achievement was real and the advantages were real too.
To criticise the family for the advantages it handed him.
steps.answer: To set up the whole film: the achievement was real and the advantages were real too.
steps.why: Everything that follows is about the family, and the last line returns to the question rather than settling it.

steps.title: Write a short biography.
steps.sub: 180–220 words. Write about one person's life — somebody you know, somebody in your family, or a public figure. Include at least one turning point, marked with a conditional.
steps.placeholder: … was born in … , into a family that …
steps.html:
• Open with birth and background in one sentence.
  • Give the events in order, in the past simple.
  • Mark one turning point with a conditional.
  • Use <i>in retrospect</i> or <i>with hindsight</i> once.
  • Close with a counterfactual you decline to settle.

Useful language

  • … was born in … , into a family that …
  • If it weren't for … , she would probably never have …
  • In retrospect, that turned out to be …
  • If he hadn't … , the … could have looked quite different.
  • She wishes she had … , though she has never said so directly.
  • Who knows? Things could have been very different.
steps.modelHtml:
My grandmother, in nine lines and one turning point

She was born in 1937 in a village that no longer exists, into a family that had already lost most of what it had. She left school at fourteen because there was nobody else to look after her brothers, and she never went back, which she mentioned about once a decade and never as a complaint.

In 1961 she took a job in the laboratory of a factory in Temirtau, as a cleaner. Within four years she was running the sample room, having taught herself everything on the night shift out of a borrowed textbook. If it weren't for a supervisor who noticed and said something, she would have gone on cleaning for thirty years.

She retired in 1992, two months before the money stopped being worth anything, which in retrospect was a blessing in disguise and did not feel like one.

She wishes she had finished school. She has said so exactly twice. If she had, who knows — but I suspect she would have been much less interesting.
